rationale: A wins because it finds the grown-up buyer story: "Airbnb builds a travel-manager console to get short-term rentals written into company policy." That is the cleanest route into a corporate-travel trade piece because it gives the reporter a protagonist, a policy question, and a concrete proof ask. B's "Airbnb builds a business-travel product on top of hosts, not hotels" is sharper copy, but it walks past the travel manager who actually makes this launch matter. B is good; A is more useful in the room where the pitch gets decided.
gaps_in_A: "Airbnb goes after managed corporate lodging spend with a tool it gives away" overreads "free for travelers." Free to the traveler is not the same as free to the employer, host, or partner, and A knows it because its own proof ask has to clean up the mess.
"people who are often one-property operators" imports a host-profile claim that is not in the update. Fine as a reporting question, sloppy as a premise.
"Next step: `meanest-editor`" is the wrong process label. The real next move is proof collection around a named customer, base number, badge supply, or partner confirmation, then journalist fit.
gaps_in_B: B misses the strongest obvious angle: the travel-manager console and whether Airbnb gets written into company travel policy. That is where "central dashboard, consolidated billing" has its cleanest buyer and beat.

"expense rails as distribution channel for anything a company buys on the road" inflates a Concur/Ramp integration into a category thesis. That sentence is trying to found a trend before the facts have paid rent.
"the fastest-growing segment may still be a rounding error against room nights" is vivid, but the update only gives "off a small base." Ask for the denominator; do not decorate the absence.
"supply base it does not own or control" is probably true of Airbnb as a business, but it is not supplied in the update. For a blind angle set, that belongs as a question, not a loaded premise.
